title: Control Hazards & Branching
summary: The cost of not knowing the next instruction to fetch, and the spectrum of fixes from stalling to static prediction.

slides.markdown:
A **control hazard** is the pipeline not knowing which instruction to fetch next, because the answer depends on a branch that hasn't resolved yet. Every cycle spent waiting, guessing wrong, or flushing bad work is a control-hazard cost.

Unlike data hazards (fixed by forwarding, near-free) and structural hazards (fixed by duplication, one-time cost), control hazards are the hardest to eliminate — they're the reason branch prediction exists as an entire subfield of CPU design.

slides.subTitle: Not knowing the next PC
slides.markdown:
A branch instruction is fetched and decoded like any other, but its outcome — taken or not-taken, and to which target address — typically isn't known until it reaches EX, several stages after fetch already needed to know what to fetch *next*.

Meanwhile the pipeline has already fetched (and possibly started decoding) whatever instruction happened to follow the branch in memory — which may or may not be the instruction the program actually intended to run next.

slides.subTitle: Stall until resolved
slides.markdown:
The simplest possible fix: freeze fetch entirely the moment a branch is detected, and don't fetch anything new until the branch resolves in EX. This is always correct — no wrong-path work is ever done — but it's expensive: every branch costs several idle bubble cycles, and branches are common (roughly one in every five to seven instructions in typical code).

At, say, a 3-cycle stall per branch and a branch every 5 instructions, that's a large chunk of total cycles spent doing nothing — which is exactly why nobody ships this as the only fix.

slides.subTitle: Static prediction
slides.markdown:
Instead of stalling, **guess** which way the branch goes and keep fetching down that path — a right guess costs zero cycles. **Static prediction** guesses with a fixed rule, decided at design/compile time, not runtime history:

- **Always-not-taken** — assume it falls through; simplest.
- **Always-taken** — assume it jumps; better for loop backedges.
- **Backward-taken, forward-not-taken (BTFNT)** — loops predict taken, if-checks predict not-taken. One cheap heuristic, real coverage.

slides.subTitle: Flushing the pipeline
slides.markdown:
If the pipeline fetched down the predicted path and the branch resolves the other way, every instruction fetched after it is wrong and must be discarded — a **flush**.

![A pipeline flush discarding two wrongly-fetched instructions once a branch resolves against its prediction](assets/branch-misprediction-flush.svg)

Flushed instructions haven't written back yet, so discarding is safe — but fetch restarts from the correct target.

assets.alt: A pipeline flush discarding two wrongly-fetched instructions once a branch resolves against its prediction

slides.subTitle: Delayed branch slots
slides.markdown:
Some early RISC ISAs (classic MIPS) defined the instruction immediately *after* a branch as a **delay slot** — it always executes, regardless of the branch outcome. The compiler fills it with useful independent work (or a NOP), hiding one cycle of the control hazard for free.

Delayed branches fell out of favor as pipelines deepened: one slot only hides a 1-cycle penalty, but branch resolution now often takes many cycles — and baking pipeline depth into the ISA makes changing the microarchitecture later awkward.

slides.subTitle: Stalling vs static vs dynamic prediction
slides.markdown:
| Approach | Cost when right | Cost when wrong | Adapts to runtime behavior? |
|---|---|---|
| Stall | Fixed stall every branch | Same (always correct) | No |
| Static prediction | Zero | Full flush | No — fixed rule |
| Dynamic prediction | Zero | Full flush | Yes — learns per-branch history |

Stalling is simple but always pays a cost. Static prediction is free-when-right but blind to how a specific branch actually behaves at runtime. Dynamic prediction (the deep dive lives in [Branch Prediction](branch-prediction)) tracks real history per branch, pushing accuracy — and average performance — well past what any fixed static rule can reach.

slides.subTitle: Misprediction cost grows with pipeline depth
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A branch misprediction costs about the same, small number of cycles no matter how the CPU is built."

**Why it's wrong:** the flush penalty equals however many stages sit between fetch and where the branch actually resolves. A shallow 5-stage pipeline resolving in EX flushes only 2 instructions; a modern 15-20 stage pipeline flushes far more on every misprediction.

**Correct model:** deeper pipelines raise the *stakes* of every misprediction — exactly why the deepest pipelines invest most heavily in accurate dynamic prediction.
